When I got to the gate, the plane had already left.
I was nervous because I had never flown alone before.
It dawned on me that I had left my passport at the hotel.
By the time we arrived, the restaurant had closed.
You look tired, Daniel. Are you OK?
I am. Long story short, I was stranded at the bus station last night.
Oh no! What happened?
When I got there, the last bus had already left. I had looked at the old timetable.
So what did you do?
Out of the blue, my neighbor drove past. He had seen me from the road.
That was a close call! What time did you get home?
At midnight, but just in the nick of time. It started to rain as I opened the door.
When I got there, it had already started.
It dawned on me that I had made a mistake.
Long story short, it all worked out.
It was a close call.
It was a blessing in disguise.

Good storytellers do something simple. They do not tell everything in order. They start with the big moment, and then they go back. When I got to the gate, the plane had already left. In one sentence, you know two things: what happened, and what had happened before. That second part is the backstory, and English has a special form for it, had plus the past participle. I had forgotten. She had never seen the sea. We had already eaten. Try it the next time you tell a story. Start with the moment that surprised you. Then go back and explain. Your listener will stay with you, because now they want to know how it happened.

A few years ago, my wife and I drove three hours to a friend's wedding in the mountains. We were late, of course, because we had stopped twice for coffee. When we arrived, the ceremony had already started, so we sat quietly at the back. The bride was beautiful, but something was strange. I did not recognize anyone. Not one person. Then it dawned on me. We had come to the right church, but on the wrong day. Our friend's wedding was the next Saturday. We had walked into a stranger's wedding. Long story short, the family was very kind, they invited us to the party, and we danced until two in the morning. The next Saturday, we were the first guests to arrive.

First, I start with the big moment: when I got to the gate, the plane had already left. Then I go back in time: I had read the ticket wrong. After that, I say how I felt: I was stranded, and my phone was almost dead. Next, I tell the twist: out of the blue, a stranger offered to help. In the end, I give the lesson: long story short, it was a blessing in disguise.
